BENEOS.Wiki.Page.requirements.Body:
Beneos maps lean on a handful of free companion modules. Install and activate all of them before you load a Beneos scene, or teleporters, levels and effects simply will not fire.

The five you need

Monks Active TilesRuns the interactive tiles on our maps: world-map jumps, traps, buttons. Deep dive.
Point of Interest TeleporterThe right-click scene jumps the GM uses to move between overview, scenery and battlemap. Deep dive.
FXMasterPaints weather and atmosphere onto a map: rain, fog, embers, snow. This is how you change a scene's mood. Deep dive.
Multilevel TokensMoves tokens between floors and powers the player-facing navigators. Deep dive.
libWrapperA small library the others build on. No settings, just keep it on.

Turn them on

Open Game Settings, Manage Modules, tick all five, save. If a teleporter icon does nothing, or a map looks flat and silent, a required module is off. That is almost always the cause.

Where the content comes from

You do not need a separate marketplace app. Every Beneos map, creature, spell and item installs straight from the Beneos Cloud window inside Foundry. Set up the five modules here, then open the Cloud and start pulling things in.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.dm-navigation.Title: DM Navigation & Controls
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.dm-navigation.Search: dm gamemaster navigation teleporter journal notes overview map scenery battlemap compass info handout sound ambient doors
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.dm-navigation.Body:
The standout feature of Beneos Battlemaps is that the maps are connected. Most releases bundle several maps for one location, all tied to an overview map. As DM you jump from a map to its scenery, or pull back to the overview for a bird's-eye view. The Point of Interest Teleporter module handles this, and we set it all up in advance. This page just covers the interactions. Want to build your own links? There is an optional deep dive in POI Teleporter.

Note: every icon here is invisible to players. They exist for the DM, to make navigation work without any technical know-how.

Right-click to travel

Maps carry placed journal entries. Right-click one and you get two DM options:

  • View Scene switches only the DM to the target scene.
  • Activate Scene moves all active players to the target scene.

Make icons visible

No journal icons on your maps? Turn them on. In the Foundry toolbar on the left, click the banner (notes) icon, then the pinhead icon labeled Toggle Notes Display. All journal icons stay visible.

What the icons mean

Every Beneos release uses the same icon for the same job. Learn them once and every map reads the same way.

IconMeaning
Overview map. Leads to the pack's main overview map.
Regional map. Highlights the specific region or kingdom within Beneos' fantasy world, Escalia. Gives context, whether it is a kingdom or a place like Barovia.
World map. A gateway back to the global map, with jumps to continents or kingdoms. This map uses Monks Active Tiles, so keep all required modules active.
Optional player handouts. Double-click for an immersive shot of the current map. Optional, and good for highlighting story-relevant aspects.
Scenery. An immersive, cinematic view of the current battlemap, ideal for role-playing moments.
Battlemap. The tactical view of the current scenery, for combat or deeper exploration.
Help. Links back to this guide.
Player intro. Specially produced video sequences for an immersive intro to a scene, where available.
Compass. Helps you orientate on battlemaps and sceneries, especially when sceneries offer different perspectives.
DM navigator. Placed on the edges of battlemaps to point toward the target scene, giving you a sense of direction.
Info. Some maps add tips or information for the DM, always in the top-left corner.

Related pages

For how players move between maps, see Player navigation. For map music and effects, see Ambience and sound. For the maps themselves, see Battlemaps.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.player-navigation.Title: Player Navigation & Controls
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.player-navigation.Searc: player navigation navigator teleporter levels move walk pause mlt compass
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.player-navigation.Body:
Players move between maps too, not just DMs. Their character actors travel on their own at specific points on the map, with no DM input needed. This runs on the Multilevel Tokens module, so make sure it is installed and active. Using it is dead simple. Want the technology, or to place your own navigators? Read the Multilevel Tokens deep dive. You do not have to, since we prepared everything for you.

How player teleporters work

Multilevel Tokens connects two places: an origin and a destination. We have pre-set where each player teleporter leads. Every teleporter field (visible only to DMs) carries a journal icon. A player clicks it, their character token jumps from origin to destination, and the scene changes for that player alone. If the DM clicks a journal icon in a teleporter zone, every token moves, player and non-player alike.

You are not obligated to let players roam freely, but it can drive exciting, narratively gripping exploration. Keep track of where each player is. When a player announces a scene change, that is your cue to describe the new location properly. Two icon types control the teleporters.

What the icons mean

IconMeaning
Player navigator. The standard icon players see once they get close enough. They cannot see it through walls; they must reach the scene exit to interact. If a player clicks it while a character they control stands in the teleport zone (invisible to them), that character travels to the target scene, and the scene changes for that player alone.
Hidden DM navigator. Same effect as the player navigator, but invisible to players and unusable by them. It serves non-obvious paths: secret doors, routes to be discovered or opened later. When you decide players can move on, click it and they teleport to the destination. Great for traps, cleared paths, cracked doors.

Who sees which icons

Players see a journal icon only if its journal has been released to them or to all players. Place five icons but release each journal to a single player, and each player sees only their own. Use this to give players private notes, or to keep DM navigation separate from player navigation.

Set a journal's permission like you would a token's. Open the journal browser via Journal in the top-right navigation bar. Right-click the journal and choose Configure Ownership. All Players grants everyone in the world access (DMs excluded). Below that, set per-player rules. Usually you grant the intended player permission and leave the rest alone.

  • Owner: full reading and editing rights.
  • Observer: can see the journal, cannot edit it.
  • None: can neither see nor edit it. This is the default for all DM navigation journals, like the Point of Interest Teleporter.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.poi-teleporter.Title: Point of Interest Teleporters

BENEOS.Wiki.Page.poi-teleporter.Body:
Before you read: none of this is needed to use Beneos Battlemaps. Everything is set up for you and works out of the box. This deep dive is for anyone who wants to add Point of Interest functions to their own maps, or is just curious how it works.

What POI does

Point of Interest Teleporter (PoI), like Multilevel Tokens, is rock-solid: it handles thousands of links without complaint. PoI links maps and scenes for the DM, not the players. It gives you navigation across thousands of Beneos scenes and worlds without losing track. Every scene and release follows the same pattern, and teleporters for the same purpose always use the same icons and names.

We wanted to ship experiences, not just maps. A map feels like part of a larger whole only when it is connected to one. That is the job of Point of Interest Teleporters: they take you to overview scenes, the world map, and onward to another zone, to intro sequences, to sceneries. Any DM navigation beyond plain Foundry runs on PoI.

How POI works

PoI works through journals. Normally a journal stores notes or story text. For PoI, the journal itself is the information. In a scene's Scene Configuration, pick a journal under Journal Entry in the Ambience section. That journal is now linked to the scene and gives PoI what it needs. Every scene (battlemap, scenery, intro) has its own unique journal. That is why the Beneos Battlemaps folder in the journal explorer holds so many journals: they store nothing, they just serve as links for PoI.

Drag one of these journals onto the canvas and right-click it (1) for options. View Scene takes you (not your players) to the journal's scene. Activate Scene forces everyone, you included, onto the target scene. So each PoI teleporter targets exactly one scene. Assign a journal in Scene Configuration and that journal represents that scene. Wherever you place it, right-clicking takes you there.

Make icons visible

No journal icons on your maps? Turn them on. In the Foundry toolbar on the left, click the banner (notes) icon (1), then the pinhead icon labeled Toggle Notes Display (2). All journal icons stay visible.

Destination not installed? Install it on the spot

If a teleporter points at a release you have not installed yet, you do not have to hunt for it. Right-click the icon and choose Install Missing Pack. A dialog shows the release, lets you pick 4K or HD with the download size (1), and installs it straight into your world. When it finishes, right-click the icon again and travel. This is GM-only.

Find what is missing

Running a big imported world and not sure which links are broken? Open Module Settings, Beneos Teleporter, Open Audit Window. It scans every scene and lists each broken or missing teleporter: the source scene, the intended target, the status, and the release you would need to install. Go to Source jumps the canvas to the note so you can fix it.

Troubleshooting

A teleporter that lands on the wrong scene is usually one of three things: no journal assigned to the icon, the journal not assigned to a map, or the same journal assigned to more than one map. Each journal must belong to exactly one scene.

For the DM-facing icons in play, see DM navigation. For player-driven movement, see Multilevel Tokens.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.multilevel-tokens.Title: Multilevel Tokens
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.multilevel-tokens.Searc: mlt multilevel tokens levels regions teleport clone players navigator floors
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.multilevel-tokens.Body:
Before you read: none of this is needed to use Beneos Battlemaps. Everything is set up for you and works out of the box. This deep dive is for anyone who wants to add Multilevel Tokens functions to their own maps, or is just curious how it works.

What MLT does

Multilevel Tokens (MLT) is an old module that still works flawlessly. It teleports tokens from one place to another, letting player and DM creatures move independently between maps. Why MLT over newer modules that also teleport tokens? Because of how it works. MLT does not use Foundry IDs, it uses its own identifiers. That means, unlike Monks Active Tiles, we can link two releases even when they are not part of the same pack. Download Pack A, then later Pack B, and they work together automatically. With Monks Active Tiles you would have to download every map as one giant release or maintain every teleporter by hand, which is no fun across several thousand scenes. Trust us.

How MLT works

Everything in MLT works through drawings, shapes made with the Drawing Tool in the left toolbar. We call them MLT fields. Setting up and linking them is simple and error-free.

With MLT active, a drawn shape's settings (Beneos always uses rectangles) gain a new tab called Multilevel. Set everything each teleporter needs here, per field. Tip: copy shapes with Ctrl+C and paste them onto other scenes.

  1. Source or destination. MLT sends tokens from a source field to a destination field. Check Out to teleport from this field. Check In to teleport into it. Check both for two-way travel.
  2. Teleport identifier. The core of MLT. Enter any text, but keep it logical. When a token leaves this field, the identifier points to the destination: the token goes to the other field with the same identifier. Only two fields should share an identifier. Three or more and MLT picks at random, which causes errors. In short, source and destination are paired by sharing an identifier.
    1. The Beneos naming convention is ReleaseNumberA-MapNumberA_ReleaseNumberB-MapNumberB with leading zeros, smaller number on the left. For example 76-04_76-05, or 64-04_76-01.
  3. Activate via Map Node. With this on, the field stays inactive even when tokens enter it. Only a click on a journal icon inside the field triggers the teleport. This matters because MLT fields are usually invisible and players might otherwise change scenes by accident. So we put a unique journal icon on every field: it tells players they can leave the map here, and acts as the button if they choose to.
  4. Token cloning. Rarer but neat. Cloning shows the tokens from another MLT field on the current surface (or the reverse) without teleporting them. Move a token on Map A and it also moves on Map B. Great for seeing first-floor tokens while you stand on the second. Source and destination fields share the same identifier as always. Source is the field tokens are displayed from (the first floor here), Target is where they show (the second floor).

Follow your players

When a player steps through a teleporter, you get a private chat card: who teleported, to which scene, and a View Scene button that jumps you right to them. No more wondering where the party wandered off to. It is on by default; toggle it under Notify GM on teleport in the module settings if you ever want it off.

Add a teleport sound

Want players to hear something when they use a teleporter? Open the In field's Drawing Config, go to the Multilevel tab, and set a Teleport sound. It plays for the players who travel and for you when the teleport fires. A small touch that sells the moment.

For how this looks to players, see Player navigation. For DM-side scene jumps, see POI Teleporter.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.cloud-window.Title: The Beneos Cloud Window
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.cloud-window.Search: cloud window search engine browse tokens items spells battlemaps filters grid list resolution install
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.cloud-window.Body:
The Beneos Cloud window is the one place you browse, preview and install everything Beneos: creatures, loot, spells and maps. It is a storefront and an installer in one, and you never leave Foundry. What you install lands straight in your world.

Open it

Click the Beneos icon (1) in Foundry's left toolbar (the vertical strip on the canvas). Leave the window open while you work and drag things out of it as you go.

The tabs

Five tabs (1) run across the top of the window:

  • Home: news, the patch log, and where you sign in.
  • Creatures: 2.5D and top-down tokens, each with its actor and codex page.
  • Maps: the animated, fully built battlemap scenes.
  • Loot: items and gear, with their origins.
  • Spells: ready to drop on a sheet.

Find things: the sidebar

The left rail (1) filters whatever tab you are on. Faction, rarity, creature type, biome, source (Patreon, Free, Shop). For maps it also carries the 4K or HD switch (2), pick HD on a lighter machine (why). Toggle list or grid to taste.

Open and install

Click any result and a drawer slides out (1) with the description, a preview, and Install (2) (full flow in installing content). In a hurry? Drag a map, creature or item straight onto the canvas or the Actors sidebar.

Keep it tidy

  • Update available: a newer version of something you own shows a badge. Reinstall to update, nothing to remove first.
  • Orphan cleanup: a maintenance tool clears lost actors and items so your sidebars stay clean.

Locked content

The window shows the whole catalog, including what your membership does not cover yet. Locked content is marked with a Join prompt, so you always see what a membership would add. To unlock, sign in; to see what each tier gives, read Patreon tiers and the shop.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.login-accounts.Title: Login & Your Beneos Account
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.login-accounts.Search: login account passwordless email patreon shopify membership sign in connect disconnect
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.login-accounts.Body:
One Beneos account unlocks everything you own, in Foundry and on the webshop. No password: just your email and a one-time code, about a minute.

Why you need one

Your account is how Beneos knows what is yours. Patreon membership, shop purchases, free releases: they all attach to your account, and the module reads that list to decide what you can install. No account, nothing unlocks. Even a free one is worth it: there is free content of every kind, free maps, creatures, loot and spells.

Use your Patreon email

This is the one thing to get right. Sign in with the same email address you use on Patreon. When you do, your membership links automatically the moment you first log in, and your content is just there. Different email? See the fix at the bottom of this page.

First login creates your account

There is no separate sign-up. You sign in for the first time from inside Foundry, and the moment you type your email and confirm, your account is created on the spot. That is it. Two places to start it:

  • Module Settings: Foundry settings, find the Beneos module, click Sign in to Beneos Cloud.
  • Cloud window: open the Cloud window and sign in (1) from the Home tab.

The login, step by step

  1. Click Sign in and type your email (the Patreon one), then Send code.
  2. Beneos emails you a one-time code. No password anywhere.
  3. Enter the code (1) and Verify. The first time, this creates your account on the spot.
  4. Beneos checks your memberships in the background, and you are in. The footer now shows Connected.

No code? Check your spam folder, wait out the short cooldown, and send it again (2).

Used a different email than Patreon?

No problem, and no need to start over. Open Your Library on the webshop, go to your Beneos user settings, and add your Patreon email there. Both addresses then count toward your account, and your membership unlocks. More on this in linking your accounts.

What it unlocks

A free account gets the free content immediately. The two Patreons, Beneos Battlemaps and Beneos Creatures, Spells & Loot, add the rest; what each tier gives is in Patreon tiers and the shop. Locked content still shows in the Cloud with a Join prompt, so you always see what a membership would add. Signed in? Go install something.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.installing-content.Sear: install download creatures tokens spells loot items actors compendium import update
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.installing-content.Body:
Installing is a click. Pick an asset, confirm, and it is in your world, wired up and ready. Sign in first so the module knows what is yours.

Click Install

In the Cloud window, find the asset and hit Install. For maps, set the resolution first with the 4K / HD switch at the top of the Maps tab; creatures, loot and spells install at full quality. There is no form to fill in. The module checks your access in the background (locked content shows a Join prompt instead of installing), skips anything you already own, and goes straight to the download. A progress window tracks it from start to finish, and reinstalling something you already have asks first before it overwrites the scenes.

What lands in your world

The asset downloads and unpacks into your world's beneos_assets folder, then the module hooks it up:

  • Creatures become an Actor (1) in your sidebar, with their 2.5D and top-down tokens.
  • Loot and spells become Items you can drag onto a sheet.

Everything is checked on disk afterwards, so you never get a half-installed actor. If a file is missing, the module says so instead of leaving you guessing.

Updates

When we ship a newer version, its listing shows an Update available badge. Reinstall and the new version replaces the old one in place.

Next

  • Creatures and their lore: the Creature Codex
  • Gear and its powers: items and origins
  • Animated scenes: battlemaps
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.creature-codex.Title: The Creature Codex
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.creature-codex.Search: creature codex bestiary tactics lore abilities pdf read aloud download creatures
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.creature-codex.Body:
A Beneos creature is more than a stat block and a pretty token. Every monster ships with what a GM actually needs at the table: how to play it, what makes it dangerous, what to read aloud, and how to make its arrival land. The Creature Codex is where that lives. We offer 700+ creatures, 400+ from the SRD and 300+ original Beneos designs, each with its own detail page.

Get a creature into your world

Creatures come from the cloud. Open the Beneos Cloud window, go to the Creatures browser, and install the one you want. Installing creates an Actor in your sidebar with its clean 2.5D token, ready to drag onto the canvas. From there the creature is yours to run, online or off.

Opening the Codex

The Codex is a dedicated window inside the module, a route-based hub so you can jump between creatures without losing your place. Two ways in:

  • From the Cloud window, open a creature's detail page and step into its full Codex entry.
  • From the creature's actor sheet, where a button takes you straight to its page.

What a creature page gives you

Each page is split into clear sections so you find what you need mid-combat without scrolling through walls of text.

Overview

Quick orientation, led by a read-aloud combat starter: a short, evocative paragraph to read the moment the fight begins. The encounter opens as a moment, not a dice roll.

Tactics

How the creature fights. Its approach, where it wants to be on the field, what it fears, the threats it brings. Skim this before you place the token.

Abilities

Its signature, CR-scaled powers, the things that make it feel distinct instead of a reskin. The Combat Autopilot helps you track these in play.

Lore

The background that lets you answer player questions and seed the creature into your world.

Foreshadowing

Short hints to drop before the encounter to build dread, plus a death prompt for when it falls. See Foreshadowing and Immersion for using these well.

Tools on the page

  • Combat Autopilot: a per-creature helper that keeps the fight on rails. See Combat Autopilot.
  • Printable PDF: a clean single-creature PDF for the table or for prep.

Built for immersion

Beneos creatures are made to feel alive on the canvas. Tokens carry FX like drop shadows and a soft glow, and the clean 2.5D art reads instantly even in a crowded scene. The Codex pairs that presence with the words to match, so you run a monster as a scene rather than a number.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.combat-autopilot.Title: Combat Autopilot
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.combat-autopilot.Search: autopilot combat round ability tracker cooldown reminder creature encounter
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.combat-autopilot.Body:
Running a memorable monster means juggling whose turn it is, which round you are on, whether the creature already spent its big move, and whether it is making the entrance it deserves. The Combat Autopilot takes that bookkeeping off your plate. It lives on each creature's page in the Creature Codex and keeps a single fight on rails for the GM.

What it does

Tracks the round

A round counter you increment as combat moves forward. Many abilities scale or trigger by round, so the number stays front and center and you never second-guess where the fight stands.

Tracks ability usage

The creature's signature abilities are listed with cooldowns. Mark one used and the Autopilot tells you whether it is once-per-round or once-per-day and when it comes back. No more firing the dragon's breath two turns in a row, no more forgetting the recharge that would have turned the fight.

Nails the first appearance

The first time the creature shows up, the Autopilot offers a one-time first-appearance prompt, a cue for its debut. It helps you give the entrance weight, then steps out of the way.

How the state behaves

Tracking is scoped to the current session. Reload the world and it resets, so the next fight starts clean: fresh round count, every ability available. Nothing to clear by hand.

A GM aid, not an automation

The Autopilot is a co-pilot. It does not take actions for you: no rolling attacks, no moving the token, no spending resources. It tracks, reminds, and prompts. Every decision stays yours, by design, because the fun of running a monster is making the calls yourself.

Where to go next

  • The home for every creature's tools: Creature Codex
  • Setting up the entrance and the death beat: Foreshadowing and Immersion
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.foreshadowing.Title: Foreshadowing & Immersion
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.foreshadowing.Search: foreshadowing immersion hooks hints death prompt read aloud narration mood
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.foreshadowing.Body:
The scariest monster is the one the players sensed before they saw it. A good encounter has a build-up and a payoff, and a great one has an ending the table remembers. Every Beneos creature ships with material for exactly this: foreshadowing hints to set up the encounter, and a death prompt to close it. Run a creature as a scene with a beginning, middle, and end, not just a stat block you drop on the map.

Foreshadowing hints

Each creature comes with foreshadowing material: short, discrete hints to drop before the encounter to build dread and pace it. We deliver them as separate beats, not one block of text, on purpose. A single paragraph gets read once and forgotten. Separate beats let you space the tension over a session or several.

How to use them well

  • Spread them out. One beat now, another an hour later, a third next session. The gap between hints is where dread grows.
  • Make them earned. Tie a beat to something the party actually does: a room they enter, a body they find, a question they ask an NPC.
  • Stay restrained. A hint suggests, it does not explain. Players should feel something is wrong before they can name it.

Done right, by the time the creature appears your players already have a knot in their stomach, and the read-aloud combat starter lands on prepared ground.

The Death Prompt

When the creature dies, trigger its Death Prompt: a written description of its demise. It can carry a final line, a last word or defiant gesture, or an environmental effect, the way a thing's death changes the room around it. Instead of "it drops to zero, it's dead," you get a moment that gives the kill weight and rewards the table for the fight they just won.

Reading it tastefully

Trigger the Death Prompt only when the death matters: the dungeon boss, the creature you spent three sessions foreshadowing, the one that nearly took a player character with it. For the third goblin in a corridor, skip it. The prompt is a spotlight, and spotlights only work when you do not point them at everything.

Running a creature as a scene

Put the pieces together and a single monster becomes a three-act beat: foreshadowing builds the dread, the read-aloud starter opens the curtain, the Death Prompt brings it down. Pair them with the Combat Autopilot to keep the fight sharp, and your players stop seeing stat blocks and start meeting characters.

Where to go next

  • Where the foreshadowing and death material lives: Creature Codex
  • Keeping the fight on rails: Combat Autopilot
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.items-origins.Title: Items & the Origins
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.items-origins.Search: items origins magical archetypes ancient arcane vampiric attunement rarity named generic
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.items-origins.Body:
Magic items are more fun when they belong to something. A Beneos item is never just a name and a bonus: it carries an Origin, one of 19 magical archetypes that says where its power comes from, how it feels, and how it interacts with the rest of the party's gear. Origins are the backbone of the whole item system, feeding both set bonuses and the Item Radar.

The 19 Origins

Every Beneos item belongs to exactly one Origin. The full set:

  • Ancient
  • Arcane
  • Awoken
  • Beastforged
  • Blessed
  • Crystalline
  • Druidic
  • Dwarvenforged
  • Elemental
  • Feywoven
  • Giantforged
  • Infernal
  • Mutation
  • Occult
  • Primordial
  • Relic
  • Sanctified
  • Technoarcane
  • Vampiric

What defines an item

Beyond its Origin, each item has two traits that shape play:

  • Rarity: Common, Uncommon, Rare, Very Rare, or Legendary. Rarity feeds directly into set-bonus math (see Origin Set Bonuses).
  • Named or Generic: a Named item is a specific, famous artifact with its own identity. A Generic item represents its Origin. The two count differently for set bonuses.

The Origins gallery

The Codex has an Items tab, and at its heart is the Origins gallery (1): 19 cards, one per Origin. Each card is a full briefing on that archetype.

Open a card and you get:

  • The Origin's lore, so you can place it in your world.
  • Its set-bonus tiers, the rewards for attuning multiple items of that Origin.
  • Sample items that belong to it.
  • An attunement simulator to preview the bonuses before you hand the loot out.

The item companion panel

Every item sheet gains a companion panel that shows the item's place in the system at a glance: the Origin emblem, its tier, whether it is named or generic, and its set contribution. Players and GMs read what an item is without digging.

What Origins power

Origins are not decoration. They drive three connected systems:

  • Set bonuses: attune several items of the same Origin to unlock tiered rewards. See Origin Set Bonuses.
  • The Item Radar: a GM tool that turns Origins into an in-fiction treasure sense. See The Item Radar.
  • The Forge: imprint your own existing loot with an Origin and fold it into all of the above. See The Forge.

Getting items into your world

Browse and install Beneos items like everything else, from the Cloud window. See installing content for the full flow.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.set-bonuses.Title: Origin Set Bonuses
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.set-bonuses.Search: set bonus echo resonance perfect harmony fusion ritual rarity modifier attunement tiers
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.set-bonuses.Body:
Collecting magic items is satisfying. Collecting items that belong together is better. Beneos set bonuses reward a player for attuning multiple items of the same Origin, turning a pile of loot into a growing, themed kit. The more of one Origin a character commits to, the stronger and more characterful the payoff.

The three tiers

Attuning items of the same Origin unlocks tiered bonuses. Three tiers, by how many you have attuned:

TierAttuned itemsWhat you get
Echo of Origin1A small passive, or a once-per-day feature.
Resonance2A stronger active or passive effect.
Perfect Harmony3A capstone effect, the full expression of the Origin.

The fusion ritual

At Perfect Harmony, a character may perform a fusion ritual that combines the three items into a single artifact. Pure upside: the fused artifact still counts as three items for future stacking, so the player keeps their tier and sheds the inventory and attunement clutter of three separate pieces. A clean reward for committing to an Origin.

The Rarity Modifier

Set effects are not all flat. Many scale with the Rarity Modifier: the sum of your attuned items' rarities. Each rarity has a value:

RarityValue
Common1
Uncommon2
Rare3
Very Rare4
Legendary5

Add up your attuned items' rarities for your Rarity Modifier, capped at 15. Chasing the strongest version of a set effect means wanting not just three items of an Origin, but three powerful ones.

Named versus Generic

Named or generic status changes how an item counts toward your set:

  • Named items count toward Resonance and Perfect Harmony, so they absolutely build your tier.
  • But a named item alone does not grant the solo Echo of Origin. The opening tier comes from a generic item.

So a famous artifact slots beautifully into a built-out set, but it will not bootstrap one by itself.

The Beneos Sets tab

Every character sheet gains a Beneos Sets tab that lays out your progress. Per Origin it shows your attuned count, Rarity Modifier, active bonuses, and progress to the next tier (1). The at-a-glance answer to "what does my gear do together, and what am I one item away from."

Where to go next

  • The Origins themselves and the simulator: Items and the Origins
  • Hunting for the next item of an Origin: The Item Radar
  • Adding your own loot to a set: The Forge
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.item-radar.Title: The Item Radar
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.item-radar.Search: item radar lgc live game control ping sense compass direction distance origin gm
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.item-radar.Body:
"You sense something" is one of the oldest tools in a GM's kit. The Item Radar turns it into a real mechanic. Plant a treasure lead in the world and your players physically feel the pull toward it, in fiction, on their own character sheets. It is GM-only, and it makes item hunting a guided adventure instead of a die roll on a random table.

Push a ping (GM side)

The Item Radar lives in the Beneos Live Game Control panel, on its Item Radar tab. GM-only. To plant a lead, push a ping by choosing three things (1):

  • Origin: which Origin the distant item belongs to. Only players attuned to that Origin sense it.
  • Distance: close, mid, or far, roughly 1, 3, or 5 miles.
  • Direction: an 8-point compass heading.

Managing active pings

Pushed pings appear in an Active Pings list, fully live. As the party travels, adjust the distance and direction on the fly so the lead tracks the world honestly. Each ping carries a timestamp so you see how long it has run, and when players resolve it you end the ping.

The Sense Compass (player side)

Any player attuned to an item of that Origin sees a live Sense Compass on their sheet. It points toward the ping and shows its distance, updating as you adjust behind the screen. End the ping and the compass reads "Contact Lost," a clean in-fiction signal that the trail went cold or the prize is claimed.

Because only attuned players sense it, the radar rewards investment in an Origin: a character committed to a set becomes the party's living dowsing rod for more of it.

Running it at the table

  • Plant a ping far at the start of an arc to give the party a direction without a quest marker.
  • Tighten the distance from far to mid to close as they get warmer, and the compass tells the story for you.
  • End the ping the moment the lead resolves, so "Contact Lost" punctuates the find.

Previewing the compass

Want to show a player the Sense Compass before a real hunt? A demo toggle in settings previews it without an active ping, handy for onboarding a table.

Where to go next

  • Why attunement and Origins matter: Origin Set Bonuses
  • The full Origins system: Items and the Origins
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.forge.Title: The Forge
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.forge.Search: forge imprint anvil origin item convert echo set bonus craft
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.forge.Body:
Your campaign already has loot. The +1 sword from session two, the heirloom amulet you wrote yourself, the strange ring the party pried off a dead wizard. The Forge folds all of it into the Beneos Origins systems, so your own items gain set bonuses, treasure-sense detectability, and a place in the wider mythology, without rebuilding anything.

What the Forge does

The Forge lives in the Items tab of the Codex and is a GM tool. It imprints any non-Beneos item with an Origin. Take a plain Foundry item, give it an Origin, and it becomes a full participant in the Beneos item ecosystem.

How to imprint an item

  1. Open the Forge in the Codex Items tab.
  2. Drag the item onto the anvil.
  3. Choose an Origin from the 19 archetypes.

That is the whole ritual. The item is imprinted.

What the item gains

Once imprinted, your item picks up everything a native Beneos item carries:

  • The Origin's name and lore, woven on so it reads as part of that archetype.
  • An Echo of Origin bonus, the opening set-tier reward.
  • Full attunement-tier mechanics, so it climbs toward Resonance and Perfect Harmony alongside other items of its Origin. See Origin Set Bonuses.
  • Detectability by the Item Radar, so an attuned player can sense it across the map. See The Item Radar.
  • Set-bonus tracking, so it shows up properly in the Beneos Sets tab and counts toward tiers.

Why this matters at the table

The Forge bridges your campaign and the Beneos systems. You do not have to choose between the loot you lovingly placed and the depth of Origins, set bonuses, and the radar. Imprint your existing treasures and they join the same living web: a homebrew amulet anchors a Vampiric set, your party's signature blade pings on a player's Sense Compass, and the artifact at the end of your campaign carries the weight of a real archetype.

Where to go next

  • The Origins you can imprint: Items and the Origins
  • What imprinted items contribute to: Origin Set Bonuses
  • How players sense them: The Item Radar
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.battlemaps.Title: Animated Battlemaps & Scenes
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.battlemaps.Search: battlemap scenery animated webm video 4k hd variants intro releases install scene
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.battlemaps.Body:
Beneos battlemaps are not flat images you drop in and align by hand. They are animated, professionally pre-configured Foundry scenes. Video background, walls, lighting, ambient sound, and intro sequences are set up in advance, including day and night variants and static fallbacks where they make sense. Open a scene and it is ready to play.

What a release contains

Most releases bundle several connected maps for one location, not a single standalone map. A typical release includes:

  • An overview map that ties the location together.
  • Regional and world maps that place it in the wider world.
  • Sceneries, cinematic immersive views for role-playing moments.
  • Battlemaps, the tactical views you actually fight on.
  • Handouts, optional immersive shots you can show players.

Teleporters link all of them, so you move between them with one click. In the Scene Directory, a release lists its animated battlemap (BM) and the matching static scenery (SC) side by side (1). See DM navigation for jumping around as the DM.

Animated, with fallbacks

The maps come alive: water moves, torches flicker, weather drifts across the scene. Every animated map ships with a static fallback, so you can switch to a still image any time, for example on a weaker machine. Many maps include day and night variants too. You stay in full control of how the scene looks and runs.

How to install them

Battlemaps install through the Beneos Cloud window. Pick a release, choose 4K or HD, download. See Installing content for the steps, and Performance and resolution for help choosing 4K versus HD.

After install, the scenes land in your Scene Directory fully set up: walls, lighting, sound, teleporters, and intros all in place. Nothing to configure. To set music and ambient volume, see Ambience and sound.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.ambience-sound.Title: Ambience & Sound
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.ambience-sound.Search: ambience sound playlist ambient interface doors volume music sliders
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.ambience-sound.Body:
Beneos maps come with sound built in: ambient soundscapes, intro audio, click effects on interactive features, and door sounds. Animated maps run looping ambience playlists that start with the scene, so the atmosphere is there the moment you open a map. This page is about controlling the volume.

Where to set the volume

Simple, with one catch: you cannot set the volume for your players. Each player adjusts it on their own client. Volume lives in the Playlist tab in the top-right navigation bar.

  • The Playlist slider sets the DM's music, meaning everything played in the Playlist tab.
  • The Ambient slider is the important one. It controls intros, map sounds, and the click effects on interactive maps.
  • The Interface slider sets door sounds. If doors feel too loud, turn it down.

Because each client sets its own levels, if a player says the music is too loud or quiet, point them to their own Playlist sliders. There is no central volume the DM can push to everyone.

Related pages

For how scenes are built and what the looping ambience belongs to, see Battlemaps. For moving between scenes, see DM navigation.

BENEOS.Wiki.Page.performance.Search: performance quality resolution 4k hd static animated fps fx disable lag
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.performance.Body:
A Beneos map is a video, and video asks more of your machine than a still image does. If a scene stutters, you have a few honest levers. None of them touch quality where it matters.

4K or HD?

Most releases let you pick a resolution when you install: 4K or HD. 4K is sharper on a big high-res display but eats more disk, video memory and GPU. HD is lighter and still looks great at table distance. Not sure? Take HD, you can pull the 4K version later. You choose this in the Cloud window.

Switch to Static View

Every animated map also ships as a still. If your system cannot keep up on a scene, switch that one map to its static version, scenery or battlemap, and the stutter is gone. Nothing to re-download. In the Scene Directory, right-click the scene. The menu shows the one switch that applies to it:

  • On an animated scene you get Use Static Map (1), which swaps to the still image.
  • On the static one you get Use Animated Map, which switches back to the video.

This is the biggest single win on a weaker machine. Run static for normal play, flip to animated for the reveal.

What costs you frames

  • The animated background is the big one. It decodes video the whole time.
  • FXMaster effects (weather, particles) stack on top. More particles, more cost. Turn them down.
  • Foreground video tiles (waving trees and the like) are extra video layers wherever they sit.

On a weaker machine

  • Install HD, not 4K.
  • Play static, go animated only for the wow moment.
  • Trim FXMaster on any scene that drags.
  • Close other heavy tabs and apps. Foundry runs in the browser and shares your memory with everything else.

BENEOS.Wiki.Page.worldmap-escalia.Body:
Before you read: you do not need to build anything here to enjoy Beneos. The Escalia world map ships ready to use. This page is for GMs who want to know how it is put together, edit it, or build a world map of their own.

Terra Escalia is the world map you meet in the Setup Guide. It is the home world of the Beneos creatures and releases, one big painted continent you can hang your whole campaign on. Under the art it is not magic, just four ordinary Foundry pieces stacked on top of each other. Once you see the four, you can change any of them, or rebuild the whole thing for your own setting.

The four building blocks

1. The map itself

The base is a single large image, placed as a background and a tile on an 8000 by 8000 scene. Nothing clever. If you want your own world, this is the layer you swap: drop in your own painting and everything below still works the same way.

2. Points of interest

Every location marker on the map is a Foundry map Note with a journal pinned to it. The little castle, city, cave and harbour icons you see are those notes. Right-click one and its journal opens, which is how a player reads about a place or jumps to its scene. Each marker is labelled with the release it belongs to, for example Castle Dourcrag [Release 48], so you can tell at a glance what is installed and what is still to come. This is the same system covered in Point of Interest Teleporters, so head there to add, move, or relink your own markers.

3. The navigation bar

Top right sits a small navigation bar. It runs on Monks Active Tile Triggers: an invisible clickable tile lies over a visible text label, and clicking the invisible tile jumps you to another scene. That is the whole trick behind every Beneos menu, world map and landing page. The MATT deep dive walks through building one step by step.

4. Atmosphere: weather and light

The map is not static. Two layers give it life. FXMaster drifts clouds and a thin fog across the continent and sends birds over it, all particle effects saved on the scene. On top of that sit dozens of animated Lights, tinted and set to pulse, throwing a soft ghostly glow over the seas and the land so the whole map breathes a little instead of sitting flat.

Edit it, or build your own

Because the four layers are independent, you can touch any one without breaking the others:

  • Move or add locations: drag the map notes where you want them and link each to its journal or scene. See Point of Interest Teleporters.
  • Swap the map: replace the background image with your own world. The notes, nav bar and effects stay put.
  • Change the mood: open the FXMaster wand and trade the clouds for rain, snow, or a night filter. See the FXMaster deep dive.
  • Retune the light: add, recolour, or animate lights to match your setting. A cold blue reads as a haunted coast; a low orange reads as a burning one.

Want the map to double as a campaign hub with a full menu and sub-scenes? That is exactly what the Descent into Avernus and Curse of Strahd landing pages do, and Build Your Own Landing Page shows how to assemble one.

BENEOS.Wiki.Page.landing-strahd.Body:
Before you read: the landing page runs the moment you set it active. Everything below is for the GM who wants to work it, or rebuild it for another story. It is made for gothic-horror play and pairs with Curse of Strahd, but the pieces suit any dark campaign.

Like its infernal cousin, the Barovia landing page is a small set of scenes joined into one hub: a home page, the Barovia map, a wall of faces the party has met, a book with three tabs, and a table for the Tarokka reading. You reveal each part as the campaign reaches it. If you already read the Descent into Avernus page, most of the mechanics here will feel familiar; they share the same bones.

On this page
  • Landing page & navigation
  • The Barovia map
  • The Characters page
  • The book: quests, notes, artefacts
  • The Tarokka reading

Landing page & navigation

This is the page your players land on when they log in, so keep it active by default at the start of a session. An animated Barovia menu frames the whole hub, and from here your players reach every scene you have opened to them.

The navigation bar is built the same way as every Beneos menu: an invisible clickable tile over a visible text label, run by Monks Active Tile Triggers. To open a destination for players, show its text tile and switch its invisible trigger on; the MATT deep dive walks through it. Each scene also carries its own ambient track, which you can change or silence under the scene's Ambience tab.

Back to top

The Barovia map

A full map of Barovia, ready to sit at the heart of the campaign. Use it as the players' overview of the valley: where they are, where they have been, and where the mist still hides. It behaves like any Beneos map, so you can drop point-of-interest markers on it and link them to scenes and journals. See Point of Interest Teleporters for wiring those up.

Back to top

The Characters page

Barovia is a small place with a long memory, and the party will meet its people again and again. This page keeps track of them, grouped by where they were met: the Village of Barovia, Durst Manor, the Vistani camp, Argynvostholt, Old Bonegrinder, Vallaki, Krezk, the ruins of Berez, the Amber Temple, the werewolf den, the Wizards of Wine, Castle Ravenloft.

Every portrait is a real actor. To reveal one, pick Token Controls, click the token, then right-click and Toggle Visibility State. Players see the face and, on hover, the name, but never the stat block. Add your own villagers the same way: drag the actor in, set its token's Display Name to "Hovered by Anyone," and show it when the party meets them.

Back to top

The book: quests, notes, artefacts

The centrepiece is a book with three tabs, reached by two small sub-navigation points at the foot of the pages. Each tab is its own scene doing its own job.

Quests

The quest tab is the party's shared to-do list. The idea is simple: you jot the jobs here so your players always know what is open, without you repeating yourself. Type a quest's title into the text field with the text tool, and mark it off when it is done. Each checkbox is a tile you toggle: leave it empty, show the tick, or drop an X on it with the text tool for a job finished.

Player notes

The second tab is a plain journal, one page handed to each connected player, so everyone has their own space to scribble theories, names, and half-remembered warnings. It is the ordinary Foundry journal you already know, just parked somewhere the party will always find it.

Artefacts

The third tab tracks the three treasures that can turn the fight against Strahd: the Holy Symbol of Ravenkind, the Sun Sword, the Tome of Strahd, and the Icon of Ravenloft. Each sits hidden until it is earned. When the party gets their hands on one, pick its tile and Toggle Visibility State to reveal it on the page, so the group can watch their arsenal grow across the campaign.

Back to top

The Tarokka reading

The last page is for the Tarokka reading, the card draw that seeds each Curse of Strahd game differently. It is a laying-out surface: a spread of five card slots your players fill with the cards their reading turned up.

One honest note on what we do and do not provide. We do not ship a Tarokka deck. We do not hold the rights to the official one, and there are far too many lovely fan decks for us to pick for you. So bring your own: run your reading however you like, then replace the five placeholder tiles with images of the cards you drew. From then on the whole group can see, at any point in the campaign, exactly which fates the cards dealt them.

Back to top

Want to build a hub like this for your own campaign? See Build Your Own Landing Page, and for the navigation itself the Monks Active Tiles deep dive.

BENEOS.Wiki.Page.landing-avernus.Body:
Before you read: the landing page works out of the box. Set it active, invite your players, and it runs. Everything below is for the GM who wants to drive it well, or bend it to a campaign of their own. It is built for hell-themed play and pairs with adventures like Descent into Avernus, but nothing stops you using it for any infernal story.

The Avernus landing page is not one scene. It is a small set of them, wired together into a hub your players can walk around on their own: a home page, a headquarters table, a page of faces they have met, a hell world map, and a garage for the war machines they capture. You reveal each part as the campaign earns it.

On this page
  • Landing page & navigation
  • The Player Table
  • The Characters page
  • The hell world map
  • Regional maps
  • The Garage

Landing page & navigation

This is the first thing your players see when they log in, so keep it active by default at the start of a session. From here they reach every scene you have unlocked for them. At the beginning only the Player Table and the Characters page are open; you unlock the rest, the world map, the garage, as the story reaches them.

Session title

Give each session an atmospheric title on the landing page: a session number and a small ominous hint of what is coming. It sets the mood before a word is spoken. Grab the Drawing Tools from the left toolbar and double-click the title text to edit it. If it does not suit your story, hide the title and its bar entirely.

How the navigation works

Each button is two tiles: an invisible clickable tile sitting over a visible text label, run by Monks Active Tile Triggers. To open a navigation point for players: pick Tile Controls, nudge the invisible tile aside, right-click the text tile beneath and Toggle Visibility State to show it, slide the invisible tile back over the label and lock it, then right-click the invisible tile and toggle its active state on. Do the same on the other pages so navigation stays seamless wherever the players are.

If MATT is ever between updates

Monks Active Tile Triggers is often one of the last modules to catch up after a big Foundry version jump. For those short windows the pages ship with a backup navigation made of ordinary journal icons, the same kind used elsewhere on Beneos maps. Grant your players ownership of those journals and drag the icons onto the bar, and they can right-click to travel until MATT is current again. Ninety-nine times in a hundred you can ignore it.

Background music

Every scene here carries its own sound source that starts when you enter it. Scenes that share a track play on without a gap as you move between them. To change or silence it, right-click the scene, open Configure, and under the Ambience tab clear or replace the Scene Playlist. See Ambience & Sound for more.

Back to top

The Player Table

The Player Table is the group's headquarters, everything they need gathered on one surface. Read it as a base in a cave, a dungeon, wherever your story wants. If you are not running the official module, switch off the animated logo in the top corner and drop in your own.

Infernal contracts

When a player signs a devil's bargain, reveal that contract on the table by right-clicking its image and making it visible. Write the actual terms into a journal, share it, and drag it onto the visible contract so players can read their own deals whenever they like.

Soul coins

Next to the contracts is a small chest for tracking soul coins. Hide the tile covering it to open the chest for your players, then show or hide individual coins as their hoard rises and falls. A little counter below reads out the total at a glance, up to nineteen.

The quest log

The large book on the table is the group's shared quest log. Type quest titles with the text tool, tick the checkbox tiles as jobs are done, or mark a finished one with an X. The book takes handouts and images too, so it doubles as a pinboard for anything the party needs to remember.

Player sheets

Bottom right holds a row of player sheets, six set up for a group of six. Activate one per player, rename the placeholders to your characters, then link each sheet's hidden token to the right character through Open Configuration and Represented Actor. After that a player can double-click their sheet to open their own character, check inventory and spells, or adjust HP straight from the table. Need more than six? Copy a sheet and set it up the same way.

Back to top

The Characters page

Campaigns pile up faces fast. This page is where your players keep track of who they have met and where. The characters are grouped by location across three sub-pages, so there is room for a whole campaign's cast.

Every portrait is a real actor from your Actor directory. To reveal one, pick Token Controls, click the character's token, then right-click and Toggle Visibility State. Players never see the stat block, but once a face is visible they can read the name by hovering over it. To add your own NPC, drag the actor onto the scene, open its token configuration, and set Display Name to "Hovered by Anyone" so players can read the name once you show it.

Back to top

The hell world map

Do not let this scene overwhelm you. It carries a lot of GM machinery, but your players only ever see the landscape and their own token. Use as much or as little as your group wants; a one-shot can ignore every marker and still get a good map.

A hexcrawl through hell

The map is sixty hexes, labelled A1 to J6, each a biome of its own: desert, burning plains, lava fields. Every hex holds at least one point of interest marked by a journal icon you double-click to read. Even with no POIs touched, the grid alone runs as a survival crawl across a hellish waste. It is built on the structure popularised by The Alexandrian, extended with third-party and homebrew content, and every outside source is linked inside its own POI.

Reading the POI colours

The point-of-interest icons are colour-coded so you know at a glance where each one comes from: blue for official Descent into Avernus content, purple for free third-party material from The Alexandrian, and yellow for extra third-party content you can buy elsewhere, with links and authors named in each journal.

Revealing a location to players

When the party discovers a place, grant them the journal: pick Journal Notes, click the icon on the hex, find its title in the Journal tab, right-click, Configure Ownership, and set it to All Players Observer. Now they can open and explore it on their own. Fog of War keeps the rest hidden until their token gets there.

Two ways to play it

You can run everything on this one global map, which is plenty for most groups, or treat the six lettered regions (A to F) as six rooms of a dungeon and drop into a detailed regional map for each. More on that just below.

A simpler map, and future growth

If the detailed grid is too busy there is a stripped-down version with fewer POIs you can switch to under the tiles. And the map grows: greyed-out icons are locations still to come, and installing the matching release lights them up automatically. Hover an icon to see which release it belongs to.

Back to top

Regional maps

Regional maps are close-ups of single areas from the global map, each rendered at full quality so every point of interest reads clearly, like a level in a video game. The hex layout matches the global map exactly, so the connections are the same; only the detail changes. Your players move hex to hex as a group and can leave one region to enter the next.

At a region's edge sit navigation hexes marked by an arrow and a journal icon. A token standing there can travel the way the arrow points, and you trigger the move by clicking the journal's eye. A minimap in the top-left corner shows all the regions at a glance. On regional maps the POIs are listed down the right-hand side rather than sitting on the hexes, which stops an accidental click from teleporting anyone. Each region also has its own tilt-shift scenery, the world shown as a little diorama, if that adds to your table's immersion.

Back to top

The Garage

The garage is where the party shows off the infernal war machines they have taken. It starts empty, just an animated background, and fills up as your players earn vehicles. Five are provided; hand them out one at a time, or park your own designs here instead.

To reveal a vehicle, pick Tile Controls, use the Select Drawings tool to click the machine, then right-click and Toggle Visibility State. Do the same for its name label with the drawing tool so the plate appears beside it.

A GM trick: fold the garage, the table, and the other back rooms into the story as a pocket dimension the party can step into, a mobile base for negotiations, storage, or showing off their fleet. To stop it becoming a free safe haven, give it teeth: the place was built for devils, so it is brutally hot, and an hour inside costs a human a level of exhaustion.

Back to top

Want to build a hub like this for your own campaign? See Build Your Own Landing Page, and for the navigation itself the Monks Active Tiles deep dive.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.landing-build.Title: Build Your Own Landing Page
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.landing-build.Search: build own landing page navigation matt monks active tiles reveal toggle visibility scenes menu hub campaign
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.landing-build.Body:
Before you read: nothing here is required to use Beneos. This page is for the GM who has seen the Avernus and Barovia hubs and thought, I want one of those for my own world.

A landing page looks fancy, but it is only ever the same four ideas wearing different art. Once you can name them, you can build a hub for any campaign, or take one of ours apart and rebuild it as your own.

The recipe

  1. A set of scenes. One home page plus a scene for each thing your players need: a map, a headquarters, a cast page, whatever your story wants. A landing page is just these scenes grouped in a folder.
  2. A navigation bar. On every scene, a small menu that jumps to the others. This is the one moving part, and it runs on Monks Active Tile Triggers.
  3. Reveal on demand. Content that starts hidden and appears when the party earns it: an NPC, a contract, an artefact, a vehicle. In Foundry that is nothing more than a tile or drawing you right-click and Toggle Visibility State.
  4. Points of interest. On the map scenes, journal markers players can open, and travel through. See Point of Interest Teleporters.

Build it step by step

1. Lay out your scenes

Decide what your hub needs and make a scene for each, plus a home page. Keep them together in one Scene folder so the set is easy to find and move. The fastest start is to copy one of our landing pages and swap the art, since the wiring is already done.

2. Wire the navigation

Give the home page a row of buttons, one per scene, then repeat that bar on every scene so players can move freely from anywhere. Each button is an invisible clickable tile over a visible text label, with a Change Scene action behind it. The Monks Active Tiles deep dive has a full walkthrough for building a navigator, and copying an existing button is by far the easiest way in.

3. Set the home page active by default

Make the home page the scene players see when they log in, and keep it active at the start of each session. From there they reach everything you have opened to them.

4. Hide what is not earned yet

Start with only the essentials visible, and keep the rest hidden. As the campaign moves, reveal a navigation point, an NPC, or a reward by toggling its visibility. That slow unveiling is what makes a hub feel alive instead of a static menu.

5. Dress it up

A landing page is a stage, so light it. Add an ambient track under the scene's Ambience tab, and use FXMaster for weather and mood. A session title on the home page, edited with the drawing tools, sets the tone before anyone speaks.

Link a spot to its guide

You can drop a help marker anywhere on a scene that opens the documentation straight to the right place, so a curious player clicks once and lands on the exact guide. Place a map Note with the Beneos help icon, then use its Label to point it:

  • Just the docs: a plain help note (no marker) opens the documentation front page, the same as the help icon on every Beneos scene.
  • A specific article: add @doc[landing-avernus] to the label and it opens that article.
  • A specific section: add @doc[landing-avernus#la-garage] and it jumps straight to that part of the article.

The @doc[...] marker is never shown on the map; only the text before it is, so a label like Garage guide @doc[landing-avernus#la-garage] reads simply as "Garage guide". The page name is the article's key from the documentation sidebar, and the section names come from each article's own headings. Left click or right click both open it.

Learn from the ones we shipped

The quickest teacher is a working example. Open the Descent into Avernus hub for the full toolkit, a headquarters table, a hexcrawl world map, a garage of rewards, or the Curse of Strahd hub for a book of quests and a wall of faces. Take the parts that fit your story and leave the rest.

BENEOS.Wiki.Page.library-overview.Body:
Your Library is your home base on the web. The Cloud window brings content into Foundry; the library is where you review what you own, grab downloads, and manage your account.

Get there

Go to beneos-battlemaps.com, sign in, open Your Library. Everything you own or can access, Patreon or shop, is gathered in one view.

The four sections

A sticky bar (1) follows you as you scroll:

  • Library: browse everything you can access.
  • Orders: your shop purchase history.
  • Account: profile and connections.
  • Membership: your Patreon tier.

The browser

The library groups your content into Animated Battlemaps, Creatures, Spells and Items (1) (Adventures are coming). Each entry carries ownership and tier badges plus a download button, so you see at a glance what is yours and at what level.

Two ways to get content

  • In Foundry: install from the Cloud window. Easiest for most maps and tokens.
  • From the web: download the ZIP from your library. What each tier unlocks is in Patreon tiers and the shop.

BENEOS.Wiki.Page.tiers-downloads.Body:
Beneos runs on two Patreons and a shop. Which one you want depends on one thing: how you actually play. Here is the whole picture, short.

Beneos Battlemaps: two tiers, two ways to play

This Patreon has two separate tiers. They are not stacked. Pick the one that matches your table.

TierYou getPick this if
Tier 1, TableplayThe map as a high-resolution video (MP4)You play at a physical table, or in a VTT that is not Foundry
Tier 2, FoundryVTTThe finished, animated Foundry scene, one click into your worldYou run your games in Foundry VTT

Run Foundry? Tier 2 is the one. The whole scene arrives built: walls, lighting, sound, teleporters, all of it. Tier 1 hands you the raw map video instead, which is what you want on a TV at the table or in another VTT.

Beneos Creatures, Spells & Loot: the All Unit tier

One Patreon, one tier. The All Unit tier unlocks everything we make on that side: every creature, every spell, every item. You install them straight into Foundry from the Cloud window, and they come with their codex pages, origins and the rest.

The Beneos Shop

Want a single release without a membership? The Beneos Shop lets you buy one map or creature and keep it for good. It is still coming online, so treat it as the second door for now, not the main one.

Free

A free Beneos account already gets you free content of every kind: free maps, creatures, loot and spells, plus still images. It costs nothing and it is the easiest way to see whether Beneos fits your table.

In your webshop library, each release offers both downloads side by side: the Tableplay video (1) and the Foundry scene (2).

How you actually get it

Inside Foundry, open the Beneos Cloud window and install what you own. Prefer files in hand? Download the ZIP from your webshop library. Either way, make sure your accounts are linked so your access is recognised.

Download links are tied to your account. Do not share them, they carry your name and your access.
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.account-linking.Title: Linking Patreon, Shopify & Foundry
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.account-linking.Search: link account patreon shopify foundry membership email connect orders billing
BENEOS.Wiki.Page.account-linking.Body:
Beneos lives in three places: the Foundry module, your Patreon, and the webshop. One thing ties them together, your email. Get the same address connected everywhere and your content unlocks consistently. Get it wrong and things look locked that you actually own.

One email, everything you own

Entitlements are keyed on email. Three addresses resolve to the same account:

  • Your webshop (Shopify) email.
  • Your Patreon email, which syncs about every 20 minutes.
  • The email you sign in with in Foundry (how to sign in).

Match all three and the module and the webshop know exactly what is yours. In Your Library, both Beneos Patreons then read as connected: Battlemaps (1) and Creatures, Spells & Loot (2).

Manage it in Your Library

Open Your Library on the webshop. The sub-navigation has what you need:

  • Account: your profile and connections. Shopify is detected automatically, Patreon you link yourself, and your signed-in Foundry devices are listed.
  • Membership: your active Patreon tier (1), billing, and a Manage on Patreon link.
  • Orders: your shop purchases, handy for confirming a buy went through.

Locked content you should own?

Nine times out of ten it is a mismatched email.

  1. Check the same email is on Patreon, the webshop and the Foundry module.
  2. A brand-new membership can take a few minutes (Patreon syncs roughly every 20).
  3. Still wrong? See the FAQ or contact us.

BENEOS.Wiki.Page.dd-monks-active-tiles.B:
Before you read: none of this is needed to use Beneos Battlemaps. Everything is set up for you and works out of the box. This deep dive is for anyone who wants to add Monks Active Tile Trigger functions to their own maps, or is just curious how it works.

Monks Active Tile Trigger (MATT for short) is one of the most powerful automation modules for Foundry VTT. It is a companion module, not part of the Beneos Module, so make sure it is installed and active. See Requirements for the full list.

What we use MATT for

MATT is an all-rounder for automating or controlling parts of a scene. We use it for:

  • Start and stop buttons that play and pause the player intro sequences.
  • Click-based navigation on the Escalia world map.
  • Mini soundboards on some scenes (for example Barovia Village, The Church).
  • Placed buttons for traps, secret doors, or other clickable events.
  • The navigation bar for the Curse of Strahd main menu.

MATT can start animations, play sounds, jump to scenes, and much more. Covering every function here would be overwhelming, and a wiki page is the wrong format for it. To go deep, there are excellent video tutorials online. Below we walk through how we use MATT so you can build your own ideas on top.

How MATT works

Everything in MATT works through tiles. The Tile Configuration gains a new tab called Triggers. MATT runs on cause and effect: when a trigger defined in Setup is met (a click, a token entering the tile, or many other conditions), whatever is defined in Actions happens.

In this example a tile is the start and stop button for the intro sequences. The intro is also a tile, and it only plays when you click the play button tile.

Select Tile Controls in the left toolbar to click tiles on the canvas. Clicking our play button (a tile with a play-button image) lets us define under Triggers what should happen and when.

In Setup you define when the action runs. Here the tile only triggers when the GM clicks it.

Under Actions, several actions are chained to a single click. MATT runs them top to bottom. Here: the tile holding the intro is reset so it starts from the beginning (Foundry has a quirk of starting webm videos at random positions), then the intro tile is started, then the clicked tile's image is swapped so the play button turns red and reads as a stop button next time, and finally a click sound plays as feedback for all players and the DM. The swap images are defined in the Images tab.

The Images tab collects the images MATT switches between. Here just two, start and stop, swapped each click. A technical note: the two images live under different file paths. When we pack a release, the second image is not exported and would be missing on download. So the second image ships inside the Beneos Module itself, which is always installed and therefore always available.

That was one example. To build your own ideas, inspect the tiles we use to control intros, build soundboards, or trigger traps. With a little creativity you can make genuinely cool interactive effects. Foreground tiles can carry MATT triggers too, covered in our foreground tiles deep dive.

Build a navigator

The clickable menus on the Escalia world map and on both campaign landing pages, Descent into Avernus and Curse of Strahd, are all the same MATT trick. A navigation button is two tiles: an invisible clickable tile sitting on top of a visible text label. The label is just there to be seen; the invisible tile does the work. Click it, and MATT jumps you to another scene.

The fastest way to make one is to copy a button that already exists, but here is the whole thing from scratch:

  1. Place a small tile where the button should sit and give it a transparent or near-transparent image. This is the clickable trigger.
  2. Double-click it, open the Triggers tab, and under Setup set it to fire on a click.
  3. Under Actions, add Change Scene, then use the small edit icon beside it to pick the destination scene from your Scene browser.
  4. Behind the trigger, place a visible text tile or button image so players know it is there to click.
  5. Right-click the trigger and toggle its active state on. That is one working navigation point.

Repeat this for each destination, then copy the finished bar onto every scene in the set. When the target scenes carry navigation back to each other, you have a menu your players can walk around on their own. That is exactly how the Beneos hubs are built, so open one and take it apart to see a full example. To reveal or hide a button as the campaign advances, show or hide its text tile and toggle the trigger's active state. For the bigger picture of how these menus fit together into a campaign hub, see Build Your Own Landing Page.

BENEOS.Wiki.Page.dd-fxmaster.Body:
Before you read: none of this is needed to use Beneos Battlemaps. Everything is set up for you and works out of the box. This deep dive is for anyone who wants to add FXMaster functions to their own maps, or is just curious how it works.

FXMaster is a companion module, not part of the Beneos Module, so make sure it is installed and active. See Requirements for the full list.

Change a map's weather and mood

FXMaster is the tool for changing how a map feels: rain, fog, embers, drifting leaves, a heavier sky. At heart it is a library of image and particle effects, configured and saved per scene. Our older releases especially (built on an older engine by a less experienced version of us) benefit from a layer of falling leaves, more contrast, or some fog and birds. FXMaster shapes a scene in post toward the look you imagined. You can completely change the mood of one map: blue fireflies plus a night filter turn a bright daytime forest into a Feywild, and heavy fog can make the same forest feel like the Svalich Woods from Curse of Strahd.

How to use FXMaster

Easy to reach, easy to use. With FXMaster active, a new icon appears in the left toolbar, the magic wand. The two settings you will use most are Particle Effects and Filter Effects, both saved per scene.

Particle Effects

This is everything that adds movement to the map. Each effect has settings like speed, density, color, and size. Send birds over the map, blow leaves in the wind, drop rain or snow onto the scene. The settings are mostly self-explanatory, so play around: it is a bit of trial and error.

Filter Effects

This is everything that changes the map itself. Adjust color, add lightning, or drop an underwater effect onto the scene. Many settings reward exploring, so try them and keep what you like.

Saving and reusing settings

Configured a scene the way you want? The filter and particle effects apply to that scene only. To carry the look to another scene, you need a macro that stores the exact settings, and it takes one click. Use the floppy disk save icon and a new macro lands in your macro list with all the current scene's changes. Right-click the macro and give it a distinctive name, because FXMaster names every saved macro the same.

Drag the macro onto your macro bar. Run it on a scene and all saved filters and particle effects apply. Delete it afterward if you no longer need it.

To strip every effect from a scene, open the magic wand toolbar and use the small trash can icon at the bottom.

Before you read: none of this is needed to use Beneos Battlemaps. Everything is set up for you and works out of the box. This deep dive is for anyone who wants to build the same sense of depth into their own maps, or is just curious how it works.

Unlike the other deep dives, foreground tiles need no companion module. They are part of FoundryVTT core, so everything here works out of the box.

What foreground tiles are

Ever wonder how tokens walk under trees, beams, or door frames? Foreground tiles. They are ordinary tiles placed over the tokens instead of under them. Tokens disappear behind anything that logically sits above them, which gives the scene real depth: a player walking under a gnarled branch, through a doorway, past an overhanging wall.

To do this we manually cut out every object taller than the players and place it as a foreground image on top. Extra work, but it is a big part of what makes a Beneos map feel like a space rather than a flat picture.

Reaching foreground tiles

To change or deactivate foreground tiles, click Tile Controls in the left toolbar. The foreground layer is hidden by default so you cannot click it by accident. Click the house icon and all foreground tiles become selectable like any other tile.

Watch out: on some maps several foreground tiles overlap (up to eight in places, say a roof plus its door beams plus a wall section). Clicking always selects the top tile. To reach one underneath, move the top one aside, click the one below, then put it back. Tiles are often locked against accidental movement, so right-click a tile and click the small lock icon to unlock it first. Usually the foreground tile is exactly map-sized, which saves you juggling lots of small tiles.

Foreground tile settings

With the foreground layer clickable via the house icon, double-click any tile to open its settings like a normal tile. You can hide a foreground tile from players, and attach automation with Monks Active Tile Trigger to run actions under certain conditions. More in our Monks Active Tile Trigger deep dive. Foreground tiles can be video files too, and partially transparent videos make lovely effects like waving treetops. Video tiles cost performance, so we use them sparingly. For keeping animated maps smooth, see Performance.

Promoting a tile to the foreground

To turn a normal tile into a foreground tile, tick Is Overhead?. Note that ticking Is Roof? alone is not enough: that only affects how token sight range is calculated from a distance, not whether the tile renders above tokens.

Occlusion modes

Occlusion Mode controls how a foreground tile behaves when a token moves underneath it. The four options:

ModeBehavior
NoneThe tile is always displayed. Right for most cases.
FadeThe whole tile fades out. Useful for a roof that should fade when tokens are under it.
RadialKeeps the tile shown and fades only a small area around the token, set with the Occlusion Alpha slider. The faded area is small and fixed, so the token can look like it sits on top of the tile rather than under it.
VisionFades only the parts a token actually sees with active token vision. In practice players see the tile clearly only when it is in shadow, which is not very intuitive.

For how all of this fits into running a scene as the DM, see DM navigation.
